A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CleanPose for category-level object pose estimation. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete supplementary material are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: v1 reports original CleanPose experiments on REAL275, CAMERA25 and HouseCat6D, alongside component ablations and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and ablation results and adds inference-seed experiments, controlled model comparisons and a debiasing analysis.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 changes the stated FIFO queue-update source from keypoint features F_kpt to output features F_f. However, v1 Figure 3 already depicts feedback from F_f, and that diagram is retained. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the procedure or corrects inconsistent prose; the remaining architecture and losses are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same pose-estimation task on REAL275, CAMERA25 and HouseCat6D. The added mug-yaw analysis examines training/test distributions without introducing a distinct dataset, population or input environment.

E2.justification: REAL275 Table 1 adds DPDN and GCE-Pose while removing SPD, DualPoseNet, GPV-Pose, 6D-ViT, IST-Net and both GeoReF combinations. CAMERA25 Table 2 drops SPD, DualPoseNet and SGPA. Table 5c replaces the non-residual MLP comparator with concatenation, and Table S6 adds a parameter-matched MLP control. This substantially revises comparator coverage; HouseCat6D comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Table S6 introduces parameter-matched controls and ResNet18 evaluations alongside ViT-S/14, with parameter count, training time and inference speed as additional evaluation measures. The existing dataset splits, pose metrics, augmentation settings and 120k-iteration training budget remain unchanged as documented.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the diagnostic evidence with parameter-matched and alternative-image-encoder controls in Table S6, inference-sampling robustness in Table S5, and mug-yaw distribution analysis in Figure S2. Table 5c also adds direct feature concatenation while removing the non-residual MLP ablation, shifting that comparison away from isolating the residual connection.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-seed statistics. v2 Table S5 reports six inference-sampling seeds, individual results and variances of 0.03 and 0.04 for 5°2cm and 5°5cm. This is a localized addition of uncertainty reporting; the seeds concern inference sampling, and training-run uncertainty remains unreported.

E6.justification: REAL275's reported 5°2cm and 5°5cm scores change from 61.5/67.4 to 61.7/67.6 in Table 1. Numerous ablation and category-wise values also change, including contrastive learning's 5°2cm result from 55.3 to 59.8 in Table 5c. Tables S5–S6 and Figure S2 add seed, controlled-performance, efficiency and debiasing findings. CAMERA25 and HouseCat6D scores are retained.

T1.justification: The structural causal model, front-door derivation, attention/fusion equations and main and supplementary loss formulas are retained. The supplementary loss section moves from B to A. No new theorem, proof or substantive formal assumption is introduced.

C1.justification: v1 presents distillation chiefly as category-knowledge guidance for generalization. v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion explicitly claim that it transfers unbiased knowledge and supplies causal supervision against feature-level bias. The overarching claims of introducing causal learning to this task and achieving leading performance on three benchmarks remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting diverse foundation-model pretraining to debiased features, excessive queue sampling to noise and redundancy, and weaker PointNet++ distillation to feature-structure matching. It interprets the new controls and yaw distributions as support for debiasing. The limitations and broader-impact discussion is unchanged, moving from Appendix A to G.

D1.justification: v2 specifies DINOv2's ViT-S/14 variant, clarifies random per-category queue initialization, and supplies parameter counts and runtime measurements in Table S6. It adds a repository address while still promising future code availability. Conversely, v1's footnote identifying the official implementation as the source of AG-Pose scores is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds GCE-Pose and more explicitly distinguishes prior-based from prior-free competitors. It removes several references, including DualPoseNet, 6D-ViT and application-motivation citations, and shortens the related-work comparison with CLIPose while retaining a comparison in Section 4.3. The fundamental positioning as a pioneering causal approach to category-level pose estimation remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, much of the introduction, distillation motivation and conclusion are substantially rewritten around data bias and causal supervision. Related-work subsections are reordered, the supplement is reorganized with limitations moved to its end, and acknowledgments and author/affiliation information are updated. These constitute substantial narrative and structural editing.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around training, inference and causal supervision, and Figure 2 relabels the mediator as keypoints. Table 1 adds shape-prior grouping, Table 5 changes placement, and Tables S5–S6 and Figure S2 are added. Most existing technical diagrams, qualitative examples and supplementary table designs are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, the parameter-matched and encoder controls in Table S6, inference-seed statistics in Table S5, and bias visualization in Figure S2 provide more informative support for the proposed mechanism. Runtime reporting also improves practical transparency. These gains outweigh the reduced baseline coverage and removal of the residual-isolating distillation ablation, but remain limited by the narrow uncertainty analysis and unresolved queue-update description.
